newsitem.title: NEPAL: Communist strike shuts down Kathmandu.
newsitem.headline: Communist strike shuts down Kathmandu.

text.p: Activists attacked cars and police detained supporters of four left-wing parties on Sunday during a general strike against a planned anti-terrorism law in the Nepali capital, police and witnesses said.
Witnesses said the strike caused merchants to shutter shops and cleared roads of taxi cabs, public buses and three-wheel motor rickshaws in Kathmandu and nearby Patan and Bhaktapur towns.
Police said protesters enforcing the strike smashed the windows of three vehicles with stones. About 30 left-wing supporters were detained in a preventive measure.
The strike was called by the National Democratic Front (NDF), a communist alliance backed by some hardline factions of the Communist Party of Nepal.
But the strike received no support from Nepal's main communist group, the United Marxist Leninist (UML) party, which dominates the ruling coalition.

The government has not published details of the planned law, but newspaper reports say a draft of the legislative bill proposed sweeping powers for police to contain a Maoist insurgency in remote parts of the Himalayan kingdom.
"The bill will negate the gains of the popular movement," NDF convenor Amik Sherchan said, referring to a bloody movement that restored multi-party democracy in the kingdom in 1990.
Nepal now functions under a British-style constitutional monarchy, which is opposed by the Maoists. The insurgents want to replace it with a government of the "working class."
The government says the proposed law is needed to contain terrorism but has not said whether it plans to introduce the bill in the current session of parliament.
Officials say at least 113 people have been killed in insurgency-related incidents and police action against hardline Maoists since the trouble began in February 1996.
Organisers of the general strike were also protesting against a recent increase in oil prices which they said had hurt the average citizen.
In June, the coalition government raised the domestic price of diesel fuel by 25 percent, kerosene by 15.7 percent and petrol by 14.7 percent.
"The fuel price rise was without any reason and it has affected the people badly," Sherchan told Reuters.

The increases in prices of diesel and kerosene were partly rolled back after strong protests from coalition partners in the government led by the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), which once had close ties to the monarchy.
